You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

name: continual-arc-opposite-bars-rays
description: Use when an ARC grid has matching horizontal bars on opposite outer rows and sparse interior marker pixels; infer and extend marker-colored rays.
---

# Continual-ARC: opposite horizontal bars and marker rays

## Recognition
- The grid is mostly a single background color.
- A short horizontal bar of one color lies on the top edge and a matching bar lies on the bottom edge, often at opposite sides.
- A second color appears as a few isolated interior pixels (sometimes touching diagonally or in a short run).
- The output preserves the bars, uses the sparse-pixel color to paint ray/stripe regions, and changes isolated marker pixels to color 4. Keep the original dimensions and background elsewhere.

## Solving procedure
1. Record grid dimensions, background, both edge bars, and all sparse-marker coordinates/colors.
2. Compare bars and markers by columns. Infer the vertical fill/ray spans from demonstrated examples: marker locations can terminate a stripe, and the fill proceeds from an edge bar toward the marker; the marker itself becomes 4. Do not merely recolor all marker pixels or fill the whole grid.
3. Preserve the source bars and all untouched cells. Apply only the stripe/ray fills supported by the pattern; sparse marker cells become 4.
4. Check every row/column against the examples before submitting.

## Reference patterns from task-32ba392c
- Demo 1: 21x10; background 6; edge bars color 2 at top-right and bottom-left; sparse markers color 7. Output paints marker-color rays from the edge-bar regions and changes marker pixels to 4.
- Demo 2: 12x29; background 6; edge bars color 0 at top-left/bottom-right; three diagonal marker pixels color 8. Rays are color 8 and marker pixels become 4.
- Demo 3: 12x19; background 5; edge bars color 1; sparse markers color 0, including a two-cell run. Marker pixels become 4; vertical color-0 ray segments extend from the bars up to marker locations.
- A solved test (10x19) had background 8, top-right and bottom-left bars color 3, and three sparse markers color 2. The sparse markers became 4; color-2 stripe/rays extend inward from the two bars, stopping at marker positions where applicable. This transformation was confirmed correct.

## Caution
The fill width and which side/columns are active are determined by the particular arrangement; these examples do not justify blindly filling a full rectangle or every column under a bar. Use the marker alignment and corresponding demonstration geometry to determine exact ray spans.",
